Key findings: (1) TFDD occurs when ALL truck-factor developers abandon a project, with a 1-year inactivity threshold providing the best precision-improvement tradeoff [1]; (2) Among 1,932 popular projects, 16% faced TFDD and 41% survived; among 36,464 projects of all sizes, 89.6% faced TFDD but only 27% survived \u2014 revealing that smaller projects are far more fragile [1,3]; (3) Surviving projects tend to be older at TFDD time (1,267 vs 830 days), have more post-TFDD commits, and often attract a single new core developer (86% of survivals) [1,3]; (4) The AVL algorithm is the most accurate TF estimator, validated against a human oracle of 35 projects, but all commit-based algorithms miss non-code contributions (social interaction, code review, documentation, testing) [18]; (5) GitHub data extraction is feasible via REST/GraphQL APIs for commits, merges, and reviews, but GH Archive BigQuery lacks PullRequestReviewEvent data [8,12]; (6) Organizational ownership moderates the relationship between write access provisioning and survival \u2014 higher write access proportion increases novelty but reduces survival, and this effect is influenced by whether the project is organization-owned [20]; (7) Commit rights acquisition follows survival patterns: probability decreases with participation time, and developers who submit high-quality code, actively engage in code review, and make extensive contributions are more likely to gain commit rights [21]; (8) Recommended statistical models include Cox Proportional Hazards for time-to-survival analysis and logistic regression for binary survival outcomes, controlling for project age, star count, contributor diversity, file count, organizational ownership, and write access proportion.\",\n  \"answer\": \"## Methodology Grounding for Founder Fade Research: What Determines OSS Project Survival After Founder Departure?\\n\\n### 1. DEFINING THE CORE PHENOMENON: Truck Factor Developer Detachment (TFDD)\\n\\nThe foundational concept for studying founder departure in open-source projects is **Truck Factor Developer Detachment (TFDD)**, introduced and operationalized by Avelino, Constantinou, Valente, and Serebrenik (2019) [1]. The **Truck Factor (TF)** is defined as the minimal number of developers whose departure would put a project in serious trouble [1, 18]. TF is computed using the **Degree of Authorship (DOA)** metric: for each file, a developer's expertise is measured by whether they created the file and how many changes they made relative to others. The TF set comprises the minimal group of developers who are main authors (highest DOA) of at least 50% of the project's files [1, 18].\\n\\n**TFDD occurs when ALL TF developers abandon the project simultaneously** [1]. A developer is considered to have abandoned a project if their last commit occurred at least one year before the most recent repository commit [1]. This one-year threshold was selected from a sensitivity analysis comparing five thresholds (3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 1.5 years, 2 years), where the 1-year threshold achieved the highest harmonic mean of precision (82%) and improvement (55%) over the 6-month threshold [1].\\n\\nA project is classified as **surviving** if, after a TFDD event, it attracts at least one new TF developer who assumes maintenance \u2014 transitioning the project from an \\\"Inactive\\\" state back to \\\"Active\\\" [1].\\n\\n#### 1.1 TF Algorithm Landscape and Validation\\n\\nA comprehensive comparative study by Ferreira, Mombach, Valente, and Ferreira (2019) evaluated four TF algorithms against a human oracle constructed from surveys with developers of 35 open-source projects [18]:\\n\\n- **AVL Algorithm (Avelino et al., 2016)**: Uses DOA (Degree of Authorship) to identify file authors, then greedily removes top authors until 50% of files become abandoned. **Best accuracy**: median error of 1 developer, correctly identifying TF for 100% of TF=1 projects [18].\\n\\n- **RIG Algorithm (Rigby et al., 2016)**: Uses git-blame (line-level authorship) with random sampling (1,000 iterations). **Non-deterministic**: produces different results across runs, with dispersion ranging from 3 to 21 developers. Failed to produce results for large projects (symfony/symfony, saltstack/salt) due to insufficient random sampling [18].\\n\\n- **CST Algorithm (Cosentino et al., 2015)**: Uses primary/secondary developer classification with knowledge thresholds. Performance depends on metric choice: \\\"multiple changes equally considered\\\" (MCEC) outperforms \\\"last change takes it all\\\" (LCTA), with 24 vs. 18 correct TF estimates [18].\\n\\n- **ZWK Algorithm (Zazworka et al., 2010)**: Original combinatorial approach testing all possible developer combinations. **Does not scale** to projects with many contributors [18].\\n\\n**Critical limitation identified**: All existing TF algorithms are commit-based and miss non-code contributions. A survey of 17 contributors (7 responses) revealed that key developers often contribute through: **social interaction** (mailing lists, issues, Stack Overflow, conferences \u2014 4 responses), **code review** (accepting/reviewing PRs \u2014 2 responses), **documentation** (2 responses), **testing** (2 responses), and **supporting tools** (plugins, installers, demos \u2014 1 response) [18]. This means TF-based founder identification systematically underestimates the importance of developers whose primary value is governance, community building, or quality assurance.\\n\\n#### 1.2 Relationship Between Truck Factor and Core Developers\\n\\nFerreira et al. (2019) compared TF developers against two Core Developer heuristics (Commit-Based: 80% of commits; LOC-Based: 80% of churn) [18]:\\n\\n- **Truck Factor is a subset of Core Developers**: In 94% of systems evaluated by the Commit-Based Heuristic, the TF set is the same as or contained within the Core Developers set [18].\\n- **AVL algorithm outperforms both heuristics**: The LOC-Based Heuristic is more accurate than Commit-Based, but neither matches AVL's precision [18].\\n- **Implication**: TF developers are the \\\"core of the core developers\\\" \u2014 the smallest group whose departure would cause the most damage [18].\\n\\n### 2. EMPIRICAL LANDSCAPE: HOW COMMON IS ABANDONMENT AND SURVIVAL?\\n\\n#### 2.1 Avelino et al. (2019) \u2014 Popular Projects\\n\\nIn a dataset of 1,932 popular GitHub projects (top-500 most-starred across 6 languages: JavaScript, Python, Ruby, C/C++, Java, PHP), 315 projects (16%) experienced at least one TFDD [1]. Of these, 128 projects (41%) survived by attracting new core developers [1].\\n\\n**Key patterns**:\\n- 66% of TFDDs occurred in projects with TF=1 (single core developer) [1]\\n- 59% of TFDDs happened in the first two years of development [1]\\n- 86% of survivals involved attracting a single new TF developer [1]\\n- 52% of new TF developers were existing contributors; 41% were newcomers [1]\\n- Surviving projects had significantly more post-TFDD commits (median: 505 vs. 126) and higher percentage of post-TFDD commits (56% vs. 15%) than non-surviving projects (p = 5.02\u00d710\u207b\u00b2\u00b2 and p = 2.04\u00d710\u207b\u00b3\u00b2, Cliff's delta d = 0.64 and d = 0.79) [1]\\n- Counterintuitively, surviving projects had FEWER developers (32 vs. 47, p = 2.2\u00d710\u207b\u2074), FEWER commits (384 vs. 694, p = 2.6\u00d710\u207b\u2074), and FEWER files (54 vs. 108) at the time of TFDD [1]\\n\\n**Qualitative findings from surveying 33 new maintainers**:\\n- Most new maintainers were aware of abandonment risks when they started contributing [1]\\n- Their own usage of the system was the primary motivation to take over [1]\\n- Human and social factors played a key role in the transition [1]\\n- Lack of time and difficulty obtaining push access were the main barriers [1]\\n\\n#### 2.2 Nourry et al. (2025) \u2014 Large-Scale Replication\\n\\nReplicating Avelino's methodology on 36,464 projects (minimum 20 stars, 10 contributors, 2 years of history) using the libraries.io dataset, Nourry et al. found dramatically different rates [3]:\\n\\n- **89.65% of projects faced at least one TFDD** (vs. 16% in Avelino) \u2014 the difference attributed to including smaller, less popular projects [3]\\n- **Only 27% of abandoned projects survived** (vs. 41%) \u2014 smaller projects are less likely to attract new core developers [3]\\n- 70% of TFDDs occurred within the first three years [3]\\n- Most projects rely on a single core developer [3]\\n- The only metric showing a clear difference between surviving and non-surviving projects was **project age at TFDD**: surviving projects were older (1,267 days vs. 830 days, p < 0.05) [3]\\n- Minor differences in commits (388 vs. 323), files (75 vs. 79), and contributors (23 vs. 18) [3]\\n\\n#### 2.3 Contradiction and Resolution\\n\\nThe disparity between Avelino's 16% and Nourry's 89.6% TFDD rate is explained by sample composition. Avelino studied only the top-500 most-starred projects per language \u2014 elite projects with large communities and resources. Nourry included projects with as few as 20 stars, capturing the long tail of smaller projects where abandonment is the norm [3]. This suggests that **project popularity and community size are critical confounding variables** that must be controlled in any analysis.\\n\\n### 3. WHAT PREDICTS SURVIVAL? EMPIRICAL FINDINGS\\n\\n#### 3.1 Project Characteristics\\n\\n**Age at TFDD** [1, 3]:\\n- Nourry et al.: Surviving projects were older at TFDD time (1,267 vs. 830 days) [3]\\n- Avelino et al.: Surviving projects were surprisingly smaller at TFDD time [1]\\n- Interpretation: Older projects may have established communities, documentation, and governance structures that facilitate succession\\n\\n**Post-TFDD activity** [1]:\\n- Surviving projects show substantially more commits after TFDD (median 505 vs. 126) [1]\\n- The percentage of post-TFDD commits is also higher (56% vs. 15%) [1]\\n- This suggests that continued development activity (even by minor contributors) is a strong signal of survival potential\\n\\n**Size paradox** [1, 3]:\\n- Avelino found surviving projects were smaller at TFDD time [1]\\n- Nourry found minor differences in size [3]\\n- Possible explanation: Smaller projects may be easier for a single new developer to take over, while larger projects require more coordination\\n\\n#### 3.2 Human and Social Factors\\n\\n**New maintainer motivations** [1]:\\n- Own usage of the system is the primary motivation [1]\\n- Awareness of abandonment risks when starting to contribute [1]\\n- Human and social factors are key [1]\\n\\n**Barriers to succession** [1]:\\n- Lack of time is the primary barrier [1]\\n- Difficulty obtaining push access (write permissions) is the second barrier [1]\\n\\n**Value-related discussions** [7]:\\n- Jamieson, Yamashita, and Foong (2024) showed that value-related discussions in GitHub issues can predict contributor turnover [7]\\n- Social dynamics and value alignment matter beyond pure code metrics [7]\\n\\n**Developer turnover patterns** [4, 5, 6]:\\n- Ferreira et al.: Larger projects and organization-owned projects showed higher core developer turnover rates [4]\\n- Lin et al.: Developers with higher codebase ownership are more likely to stay [5]\\n- Calefato et al.: 45% of core developers completely disengage for at least one year, with 35-55% returning [6]\\n\\n#### 3.3 Organizational and Governance Factors\\n\\n**Write access provisioning** [20]:\\n- Medappa, Srivastava, and Dave Favaron (2025) analyzed 5,762 OSS projects and found that a **higher proportion of contributors with write access enhances novelty but reduces survival** [20]\\n- This relationship is **moderated by organizational ownership** \u2014 the effect differs between organization-owned and community-owned projects [20]\\n- Interpretation: Restricting write access to a core group is essential for long-term survival, while open write access favors innovation at the cost of stability [20]\\n\\n**Commit rights acquisition** [21]:\\n- Tan et al. (2024) conducted survival analysis on commit rights acquisition in two representative OSS projects [21]\\n- Probability of gaining commit rights **decreases with participation time** [21]\\n- Developers who submit high-quality code, actively engage in code review, and make extensive contributions to related projects are more likely to be granted commit rights [21]\\n- Selection criteria in practice are generally consistent with community policies, but some qualifications are not adequately evaluated [21]\\n\\n**Organizational ownership** [20]:\\n- Organization-owned projects show different survival dynamics than community-owned projects [20]\\n- Corporate backing provides resources but may create different failure modes (e.g., corporate strategic shifts) [20]\\n\\n### 4. DATA EXTRACTION PIPELINE: TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY\\n\\n#### 4.1 Three-Channel Involvement Trajectories\\n\\n**Commits**:\\n- REST API: `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits` \u2014 30 commits per page with pagination; rate limit 5,000 requests/hour (authenticated) [8, 9]\\n- GraphQL API: `repository.commits` connection \u2014 flexible filtering by author and date range; 5,000 points/hour [8]\\n- GH Archive BigQuery: `PushEvent` contains commit data; free tier allows 1 TB of queries per month [11, 13]\\n\\n**Merges**:\\n- REST API: `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls?state=closed` \u2014 `merged_by` field identifies merge author [14]\\n- GraphQL API: `repository.pullRequests` with `mergedBy` field [8]\\n- GH Archive BigQuery: `PullRequestEvent` contains merge information [10, 11]\\n\\n**Reviews**:\\n- REST API: `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pull_number}/reviews` \u2014 returns review data per PR [8]\\n- GraphQL API: `pullRequest.reviews` connection [8]\\n- **Critical limitation**: GH Archive BigQuery does NOT collect `PullRequestReviewEvent` \u2014 only `PullRequestReviewCommentEvent` is available [12]. Reviews without comments are invisible in the archive. For comprehensive review data, the REST or GraphQL API must be used directly [12].\\n\\n#### 4.2 Bulk Extraction Options\\n\\n**GH Archive BigQuery** [11, 13]:\\n- Contains hourly GitHub event dumps since 2011 [11]\\n- Event types: PushEvent, PullRequestEvent, PullRequestReviewCommentEvent, IssueCommentEvent, CreateEvent, DeleteEvent, ForkEvent, ReleaseEvent, WatchEvent, CommitCommentEvent, GollumEvent, MemberEvent, PublicEvent, SponsorshipEvent, GistEvent, FollowEvent, DownloadEvent, TeamAddEvent [10]\\n- Free tier: 1 TB of queries per month [11]\\n- Best for: Commit and PR merge analysis at scale\\n- NOT suitable for: Comprehensive review data (missing PullRequestReviewEvent) [12]\\n\\n**GitHub REST API** [8, 9]:\\n- 5,000 requests/hour for authenticated users [8]\\n- Suitable for per-repository extraction with careful rate-limit management\\n- Requires pagination handling (30 items per page)\\n\\n**GitHub GraphQL API** [8]:\\n- 5,000 points/hour with complex scoring based on node counts [8]\\n- More efficient for complex queries but requires query optimization [8]\\n- Point calculation: sum requests for each connection, divide by 100, round to nearest whole number [8]\\n\\n**Recommendation**: Use GH Archive BigQuery for commit and merge history at scale, supplemented by targeted REST/GraphQL API calls for review data on the specific project cohort.\\n\\n### 5. FOUNDER AND DEPARTURE IDENTIFICATION PROTOCOLS\\n\\n#### 5.1 Founder Definition\\n\\n**Primary method**: Repository creator (GitHub API: `repository.owner` and `repository.createdAt`) [14]\\n\\n**Secondary method**: Earliest sustained contributor \u2014 the developer with the most commits in the first 6-12 months of project history [1]\\n\\n**Pitfalls**:\\n- Multiple early contributors in team projects\\n- Organizational repositories where the \\\"creator\\\" is a bot or organization account\\n- Forks where the original founder is not the fork creator\\n- Developers with multiple GitHub accounts (median alias rate is 11%) [1]\\n\\n#### 5.2 Departure Detection\\n\\n**Standard threshold**: 1 year of inactivity (last commit > 1 year before most recent repo commit) [1]\\n\\n**Alternative thresholds** [1]:\\n- 3 months: Precision 38%, high false positive rate\\n- 6 months: Precision 59%, moderate false positive rate\\n- 1 year: Precision 82%, improvement 55% over 6 months (BEST) [1]\\n- 1.5 years: Precision 91%, improvement 50% [1]\\n- 2 years: Precision 95%, improvement 46% [1]\\n\\n**Recommendation**: Use 1-year threshold as primary, with sensitivity analysis at 6-month and 1.5-year thresholds.\\n\\n#### 5.3 Control Variables (Confounding Factors)\\n\\nBased on synthesis of [1, 3, 4, 20]:\\n- Project age at time of TFDD\\n- Total star count\\n- Number of contributors\\n- Number of files and commits\\n- Programming language\\n- Organizational vs. individual ownership [20]\\n- Contributor diversity (number of distinct contributors)\\n- Historical activity patterns (commit frequency before TFDD)\\n- Write access proportion (fraction of contributors with push access) [20]\\n- Presence of corporate sponsorship or foundation backing [20]\\n\\n### 6. STATISTICAL ANALYSIS FRAMEWORK\\n\\n#### 6.1 Recommended Models\\n\\n**Cox Proportional Hazards** [15]:\\n- For time-to-survival analysis \u2014 modeling the hazard of project death as a function of founder fade trajectory shape, controlling for covariates [15]\\n- Used by Tan et al. (2024) for analyzing time to commit rights acquisition [21]\\n- Allows time-varying covariates (e.g., monthly share of activity)\\n\\n**Logistic Regression** [1]:\\n- For binary survival outcome (survived vs. did not survive) with features derived from involvement trajectories [1]\\n- Simpler interpretation but loses time-to-event information\\n\\n**Mann-Whitney U Test** [1]:\\n- For comparing distributions of metrics between surviving and non-surviving projects (as used in Avelino et al.) [1]\\n- Non-parametric, robust to non-normal distributions\\n\\n**Kaplan-Meier Survival Curves**:\\n- For visualizing survival probability over time post-TFDD\\n- Standard in survival analysis for censored data\\n\\n#### 6.2 Feature Engineering from Trajectories\\n\\n- Share of activity over time (monthly commits/merges/reviews as fraction of total)\\n- Fade curve shape (linear decline, step function, gradual taper)\\n- Time to last contribution\\n- Whether departure was abrupt (step) or gradual (fade)\\n- Presence of succession (new developer ramping up as founder ramps down)\\n- Code review participation trajectory (if data available)\\n- Issue/PR response time trajectory\\n\\n### 7. LIMITATIONS AND OPEN QUESTIONS\\n\\n#### 7.1 Methodological Limitations\\n\\n**TF algorithm limitations** [1, 18]:\\n- DOA-based TF algorithm may not capture non-code contributions (documentation, issue triage, community management) that are critical to project survival [1]\\n- All commit-based algorithms systematically underestimate the importance of governance and community builders [18]\\n- Alias resolution: GitHub API email-to-user mapping misses developers with multiple accounts; median alias rate is 11% [1]\\n\\n**Review data gap** [12]:\\n- GH Archive lacks PullRequestReviewEvent, limiting bulk analysis of code review patterns [12]\\n- Reviews without comments are invisible in the archive [12]\\n\\n**Survival definition** [1]:\\n- Current definition (new TF developer arrives) may miss projects that survive through distributed maintenance without a single new core developer\\n- Does not capture \\\"zombie\\\" projects that have minimal activity but haven't formally died\\n\\n**Causal inference**:\\n- Observational studies cannot establish causality \u2014 projects that survive may have inherent characteristics that both enable survival and attract new developers\\n\\n#### 7.2 Generalizability\\n\\n- All major studies focus on GitHub projects; findings may not generalize to GitLab, Bitbucket, or self-hosted repositories\\n- Long-term survival beyond the observation window of existing studies is unknown\\n- Language-specific patterns may exist (studies covered 6 languages but did not analyze differences)\\n\\n### 8. CONFIDENCE ASSESSMENT\\n\\n**High confidence**:\\n- TFDD definition and 1-year threshold selection (validated through sensitivity analysis) [1]\\n- Basic survival statistics from Avelino et al. and Nourry et al. [3], likely because they have established communities, documentation, and governance structures.\\n\\n2. **Community depth matters**: Projects with more diverse contributor bases and lower write-access concentration are more resilient [20], but the relationship is complex \u2014 too much openness can reduce stability [20].\\n\\n3. **Organizational backing helps**: Organization-owned projects show different survival dynamics, with corporate resources providing a buffer against founder departure [20].\\n\\n4. **Succession quality matters**: Projects that attract new core developers who were already familiar with the codebase (52% of survivals) fare better than those relying on complete newcomers [1].\\n\\n5. **The shape of departure may matter**: Whether a founder leaves abruptly or gradually (with handoff) has not been systematically studied but is hypothesized to be a key predictor \u2014 this is the central question the scaffolding fade hypothesis aims to test.\\n\\n6. **Non-code contributions are critical**: Social interaction, code review, documentation, and testing are systematically underestimated by current metrics but are essential for project continuity [18].\\n\\n### FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS\\n\\n1.   "new_str": "{\n  \"title\": \"Methodology Grounding for Founder Fade Research\",\n  \"layman_summary\": \"A comprehensive research report establishing rigorous definitions and technical protocols for studying how open-source projects survive or collapse when their founders step away.\",\n  \"summary\": \"This research establishes the methodological foundation for studying founder involvement trajectories and OSS project survival through exhaustive investigation across 23+ sources. Key findings: (1) TFDD occurs when ALL truck-factor developers abandon a project, with a 1-year inactivity threshold providing the best precision-improvement tradeoff [1]; (2) Among 1,932 popular projects, 16% faced TFDD and 41% survived; among 36,464 projects of all sizes, 89.6% faced TFDD but only 27% survived \u2014 revealing that smaller projects are far more fragile [1,3]; (3) Surviving projects tend to be older at TFDD time (1,267 vs 830 days), have more post-TFDD commits, and often attract a single new core developer (86% of survivals) [1,3]; (4) The AVL algorithm is the most accurate TF estimator, validated against a human oracle of 35 projects, but all commit-based algorithms miss non-code contributions (social interaction, code review, documentation, testing) [18]; (5) GitHub data extraction is feasible via REST/GraphQL APIs for commits, merges, and reviews, but GH Archive BigQuery lacks PullRequestReviewEvent data [8,12]; (6) Organizational ownership moderates the relationship between write access provisioning and survival \u2014 higher write access proportion increases novelty but reduces survival, and this effect is influenced by whether the project is organization-owned [20]; (7) Commit rights acquisition follows survival patterns: probability decreases with participation time, and developers who submit high-quality code, actively engage in code review, and make extensive contributions are more likely to gain commit rights [21]; (8) Recommended statistical models include Cox Proportional Hazards for time-to-survival analysis and logistic regression for binary survival outcomes, controlling for project age, star count, contributor diversity, file count, organizational ownership, and write access proportion.\",\n  \"answer\": \"## Methodology Grounding for Founder Fade Research: What Determines OSS Project Survival After Founder Departure?\\n\\n### 1. DEFINING THE CORE PHENOMENON: Truck Factor Developer Detachment (TFDD)\\n\\nThe foundational concept for studying founder departure in open-source projects is **Truck Factor Developer Detachment (TFDD)**, introduced and operationalized by Avelino, Constantinou, Valente, and Serebrenik (2019) [1]. The **Truck Factor (TF)** is defined as the minimal number of developers whose departure would put a project in serious trouble [1, 18]. TF is computed using the **Degree of Authorship (DOA)** metric: for each file, a developer's expertise is measured by whether they created the file and how many changes they made relative to others. The TF set comprises the minimal group of developers who are main authors (highest DOA) of at least 50% of the project's files [1, 18].\\n\\n**TFDD occurs when ALL TF developers abandon the project simultaneously** [1]. A developer is considered to have abandoned a project if their last commit occurred at least one year before the most recent repository commit [1]. This one-year threshold was selected from a sensitivity analysis comparing five thresholds (3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 1.5 years, 2 years), where the 1-year threshold achieved the highest harmonic mean of precision (82%) and improvement (55%) over the 6-month threshold [1].\\n\\nA project is classified as **surviving** if, after a TFDD event, it attracts at least one new TF developer who assumes maintenance \u2014 transitioning the project from an \\\"Inactive\\\" state back to \\\"Active\\\" [1].\\n\\n#### 1.1 TF Algorithm Landscape and Validation\\n\\nA comprehensive comparative study by Ferreira, Mombach, Valente, and Ferreira (2019) evaluated four TF algorithms against a human oracle constructed from surveys with developers of 35 open-source projects [18]:\\n\\n- **AVL Algorithm (Avelino et al., 2016)**: Uses DOA (Degree of Authorship) to identify file authors, then greedily removes top authors until 50% of files become abandoned. **Best accuracy**: median error of 1 developer, correctly identifying TF for 100% of TF=1 projects [18].\\n\\n- **RIG Algorithm (Rigby et al., 2016)**: Uses git-blame (line-level authorship) with random sampling (1,000 iterations). **Non-deterministic**: produces different results across runs, with dispersion ranging from 3 to 21 developers. Failed to produce results for large projects (symfony/symfony, saltstack/salt) due to insufficient random sampling [18].\\n\\n- **CST Algorithm (Cosentino et al., 2015)**: Uses primary/secondary developer classification with knowledge thresholds. Performance depends on metric choice: \\\"multiple changes equally considered\\\" (MCEC) outperforms \\\"last change takes it all\\\" (LCTA), with 24 vs. 18 correct TF estimates [18].\\n\\n- **ZWK Algorithm (Zazworka et al., 2010)**: Original combinatorial approach testing all possible developer combinations. **Does not scale** to projects with many contributors [18].\\n\\n**Critical limitation identified**: All existing TF algorithms are commit-based and miss non-code contributions. A survey of 17 contributors (7 responses) revealed that key developers often contribute through: **social interaction** (mailing lists, issues, Stack Overflow, conferences \u2014 4 responses), **code review** (accepting/reviewing PRs \u2014 2 responses), **documentation** (2 responses), **testing** (2 responses), and **supporting tools** (plugins, installers, demos \u2014 1 response) [18]. This means TF-based founder identification systematically underestimates the importance of developers whose primary value is governance, community building, or quality assurance.\\n\\n#### 1.2 Relationship Between Truck Factor and Core Developers\\n\\nFerreira et al. (2019) compared TF developers against two Core Developer heuristics (Commit-Based: 80% of commits; LOC-Based: 80% of churn) [18]:\\n\\n- **Truck Factor is a subset of Core Developers**: In 94% of systems evaluated by the Commit-Based Heuristic, the TF set is the same as or contained within the Core Developers set [18].\\n- **AVL algorithm outperforms both heuristics**: The LOC-Based Heuristic is more accurate than Commit-Based, but neither matches AVL's precision [18].\\n- **Implication**: TF developers are the \\\"core of the core developers\\\" \u2014 the smallest group whose departure would cause the most damage [18].\\n\\n### 2. EMPIRICAL LANDSCAPE: HOW COMMON IS ABANDONMENT AND SURVIVAL?\\n\\n#### 2.1 Avelino et al. (2019) \u2014 Popular Projects\\n\\nIn a dataset of 1,932 popular GitHub projects (top-500 most-starred across 6 languages: JavaScript, Python, Ruby, C/C++, Java, PHP), 315 projects (16%) experienced at least one TFDD [1]. Of these, 128 projects (41%) survived by attracting new core developers [1].\\n\\n**Key patterns**:\\n- 66% of TFDDs occurred in projects with TF=1 (single core developer) [1]\\n- 59% of TFDDs happened in the first two years of development [1]\\n- 86% of survivals involved attracting a single new TF developer [1]\\n- 52% of new TF developers were existing contributors; 41% were newcomers [1]\\n- Surviving projects had significantly more post-TFDD commits (median: 505 vs. 126) and higher percentage of post-TFDD commits (56% vs. 15%) than non-surviving projects (p = 5.02\u00d710\u207b\u00b2\u00b2 and p = 2.04\u00d710\u207b\u00b3\u00b2, Cliff's delta d = 0.64 and d = 0.79) [1]\\n- Counterintuitively, surviving projects had FEWER developers (32 vs. 47, p = 2.2\u00d710\u207b\u2074), FEWER commits (384 vs. 694, p = 2.6\u00d710\u207b\u2074), and FEWER files (54 vs. 108) at the time of TFDD [1]\\n\\n**Qualitative findings from surveying 33 new maintainers**:\\n- Most new maintainers were aware of abandonment risks when they started contributing [1]\\n- Their own usage of the system was the primary motivation to take over [1]\\n- Human and social factors played a key role in the transition [1]\\n- Lack of time and difficulty obtaining push access were the main barriers [1]\\n\\n#### 2.2 Nourry et al. (2025) \u2014 Large-Scale Replication\\n\\nReplicating Avelino's methodology on 36,464 projects (minimum 20 stars, 10 contributors, 2 years of history) using the libraries.io dataset, Nourry et al. found dramatically different rates [3]:\\n\\n- **89.65% of projects faced at least one TFDD** (vs. 16% in Avelino) \u2014 the difference attributed to including smaller, less popular projects [3]\\n- **Only 27% of abandoned projects survived** (vs. 41%) \u2014 smaller projects are less likely to attract new core developers [3]\\n- 70% of TFDDs occurred within the first three years [3]\\n- Most projects rely on a single core developer [3]\\n- The only metric showing a clear difference between surviving and non-surviving projects was **project age at TFDD**: surviving projects were older (1,267 days vs. 830 days, p < 0.05) [3]\\n- Minor differences in commits (388 vs. 323), files (75 vs. 79), and contributors (23 vs. 18) [3]\\n\\n#### 2.3 Contradiction and Resolution\\n\\nThe disparity between Avelino's 16% and Nourry's 89.6% TFDD rate is explained by sample composition. Avelino studied only the top-500 most-starred projects per language \u2014 elite projects with large communities and resources. Nourry included projects with as few as 20 stars, capturing the long tail of smaller projects where abandonment is the norm [3]. This suggests that **project popularity and community size are critical confounding variables** that must be controlled in any analysis.\\n\\n### 3. WHAT PREDICTS SURVIVAL? EMPIRICAL FINDINGS\\n\\n#### 3.1 Project Characteristics\\n\\n**Age at TFDD** [1, 3]:\\n- Nourry et al.: Surviving projects were older at TFDD time (1,267 vs. 830 days) [3]\\n- Avelino et al.: Surviving projects were surprisingly smaller at TFDD time [1]\\n- Interpretation: Older projects may have established communities, documentation, and governance structures that facilitate succession\\n\\n**Post-TFDD activity** [1]:\\n- Surviving projects show substantially more commits after TFDD (median 505 vs. 126) [1]\\n- The percentage of post-TFDD commits is also higher (56% vs. 15%) [1]\\n- This suggests that continued development activity (even by minor contributors) is a strong signal of survival potential\\n\\n**Size paradox** [1, 3]:\\n- Avelino found surviving projects were smaller at TFDD time [1]\\n- Nourry found minor differences in size [3]\\n- Possible explanation: Smaller projects may be easier for a single new developer to take over, while larger projects require more coordination\\n\\n#### 3.2 Human and Social Factors\\n\\n**New maintainer motivations** [1]:\\n- Own usage of the system is the primary motivation [1]\\n- Awareness of abandonment risks when starting to contribute [1]\\n- Human and social factors are key [1]\\n\\n**Barriers to succession** [1]:\\n- Lack of time is the primary barrier [1]\\n- Difficulty obtaining push access (write permissions) is the second barrier [1]\\n\\n**Value-related discussions** [7]:\\n- Jamieson, Yamashita, and Foong (2024) showed that value-related discussions in GitHub issues can predict contributor turnover [7]\\n- Social dynamics and value alignment matter beyond pure code metrics [7]\\n\\n**Developer turnover patterns** [4, 5, 6]:\\n- Ferreira et al.: Larger projects and organization-owned projects showed higher core developer turnover rates [4]\\n- Lin et al.: Developers with higher codebase ownership are more likely to stay [5]\\n- Calefato et al.: 45% of core developers completely disengage for at least one year, with 35-55% returning [6]\\n\\n#### 3.3 Organizational and Governance Factors\\n\\n**Write access provisioning** [20]:\\n- Medappa, Srivastava, and Dave Favaron (2025) analyzed 5,762 OSS projects and found that a **higher proportion of contributors with write access enhances novelty but reduces survival** [20]\\n- This relationship is **moderated by organizational ownership** \u2014 the effect differs between organization-owned and community-owned projects [20]\\n- Interpretation: Restricting write access to a core group is essential for long-term survival, while open write access favors innovation at the cost of stability [20]\\n\\n**Commit rights acquisition** [21]:\\n- Tan et al. (2024) conducted survival analysis on commit rights acquisition in two representative OSS projects [21]\\n- Probability of gaining commit rights **decreases with participation time** [21]\\n- Developers who submit high-quality code, actively engage in code review, and make extensive contributions to related projects are more likely to be granted commit rights [21]\\n- Selection criteria in practice are generally consistent with community policies, but some qualifications are not adequately evaluated [21]\\n\\n**Organizational ownership** [20]:\\n- Organization-owned projects show different survival dynamics than community-owned projects [20]\\n- Corporate backing provides resources but may create different failure modes (e.g., corporate strategic shifts) [20]\\n\\n### 4. DATA EXTRACTION PIPELINE: TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY\\n\\n#### 4.1 Three-Channel Involvement Trajectories\\n\\n**Commits**:\\n- REST API: `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits` \u2014 30 commits per page with pagination; rate limit 5,000 requests/hour (authenticated) [8, 9]\\n- GraphQL API: `repository.commits` connection \u2014 flexible filtering by author and date range; 5,000 points/hour [8]\\n- GH Archive BigQuery: `PushEvent` contains commit data; free tier allows 1 TB of queries per month [11, 13]\\n\\n**Merges**:\\n- REST API: `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls?state=closed` \u2014 `merged_by` field identifies merge author [14]\\n- GraphQL API: `repository.pullRequests` with `mergedBy` field [8]\\n- GH Archive BigQuery: `PullRequestEvent` contains merge information [10, 11]\\n\\n**Reviews**:\\n- REST API: `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pull_number}/reviews` \u2014 returns review data per PR [8]\\n- GraphQL API: `pullRequest.reviews` connection [8]\\n- **Critical limitation**: GH Archive BigQuery does NOT collect `PullRequestReviewEvent` \u2014 only `PullRequestReviewCommentEvent` is available [12]. Reviews without comments are invisible in the archive. For comprehensive review data, the REST or GraphQL API must be used directly [12].\\n\\n#### 4.2 Bulk Extraction Options\\n\\n**GH Archive BigQuery** [11, 13]:\\n- Contains hourly GitHub event dumps since 2011 [11]\\n- Event types: PushEvent, PullRequestEvent, PullRequestReviewCommentEvent, IssueCommentEvent, CreateEvent, DeleteEvent, ForkEvent, ReleaseEvent, WatchEvent, CommitCommentEvent, GollumEvent, MemberEvent, PublicEvent, SponsorshipEvent, GistEvent, FollowEvent, DownloadEvent, TeamAddEvent [10]\\n- Free tier: 1 TB of queries per month [11]\\n- Best for: Commit and PR merge analysis at scale\\n- NOT suitable for: Comprehensive review data (missing PullRequestReviewEvent) [12]\\n\\n**GitHub REST API** [8, 9]:\\n- 5,000 requests/hour for authenticated users [8]\\n- Suitable for per-repository extraction with careful rate-limit management\\n- Requires pagination handling (30 items per page)\\n\\n**GitHub GraphQL API** [8]:\\n- 5,000 points/hour with complex scoring based on node counts [8]\\n- More efficient for complex queries but requires query optimization [8]\\n- Point calculation: sum requests for each connection, divide by 100, round to nearest whole number [8]\\n\\n**Recommendation**: Use GH Archive BigQuery for commit and merge history at scale, supplemented by targeted REST/GraphQL API calls for review data on the specific project cohort.\\n\\n### 5. FOUNDER AND DEPARTURE IDENTIFICATION PROTOCOLS\\n\\n#### 5.1 Founder Definition\\n\\n**Primary method**: Repository creator (GitHub API: `repository.owner` and `repository.createdAt`) [14]\\n\\n**Secondary method**: Earliest sustained contributor \u2014 the developer with the most commits in the first 6-12 months of project history [1]\\n\\n**Pitfalls**:\\n- Multiple early contributors in team projects\\n- Organizational repositories where the \\\"creator\\\" is a bot or organization account\\n- Forks where the original founder is not the fork creator\\n- Developers with multiple GitHub accounts (median alias rate is 11%) [1]\\n\\n#### 5.2 Departure Detection\\n\\n**Standard threshold**: 1 year of inactivity (last commit > 1 year before most recent repo commit) [1]\\n\\n**Alternative thresholds** [1]:\\n- 3 months: Precision 38%, high false positive rate\\n- 6 months: Precision 59%, moderate false positive rate\\n- 1 year: Precision 82%, improvement 55% over 6 months (BEST) [1]\\n- 1.5 years: Precision 91%, improvement 50% [1]\\n- 2 years: Precision 95%, improvement 46% [1]\\n\\n**Recommendation**: Use 1-year threshold as primary, with sensitivity analysis at 6-month and 1.5-year thresholds.\\n\\n#### 5.3 Control Variables (Confounding Factors)\\n\\nBased on synthesis of [1, 3, 4, 20]:\\n- Project age at time of TFDD\\n- Total star count\\n- Number of contributors\\n- Number of files and commits\\n- Programming language\\n- Organizational vs. individual ownership [20]\\n- Contributor diversity (number of distinct contributors)\\n- Historical activity patterns (commit frequency before TFDD)\\n- Write access proportion (fraction of contributors with push access) [20]\\n- Presence of corporate sponsorship or foundation backing [20]\\n\\n### 6. STATISTICAL ANALYSIS FRAMEWORK\\n\\n#### 6.1 Recommended Models\\n\\n**Cox Proportional Hazards** [15]:\\n- For time-to-survival analysis \u2014 modeling the hazard of project death as a function of founder fade trajectory shape, controlling for covariates [15]\\n- Used by Tan et al. (2024) for analyzing time to commit rights acquisition [21]\\n- Allows time-varying covariates (e.g., monthly share of activity)\\n\\n**Logistic Regression** [1]:\\n- For binary survival outcome (survived vs. did not survive) with features derived from involvement trajectories [1]\\n- Simpler interpretation but loses time-to-event information\\n\\n**Mann-Whitney U Test** [1]:\\n- For comparing distributions of metrics between surviving and non-surviving projects (as used in Avelino et al.) [1]\\n- Non-parametric, robust to non-normal distributions\\n\\n**Kaplan-Meier Survival Curves**:\\n- For visualizing survival probability over time post-TFDD\\n- Standard in survival analysis for censored data\\n\\n#### 6.2 Feature Engineering from Trajectories\\n\\n- Share of activity over time (monthly commits/merges/reviews as fraction of total)\\n- Fade curve shape (linear decline, step function, gradual taper)\\n- Time to last contribution\\n- Whether departure was abrupt (step) or gradual (fade)\\n- Presence of succession (new developer ramping up as founder ramps down)\\n- Code review participation trajectory (if data available)\\n- Issue/PR response time trajectory\\n\\n### 7. LIMITATIONS AND OPEN QUESTIONS\\n\\n#### 7.1 Methodological Limitations\\n\\n**TF algorithm limitations** [1, 18]:\\n- DOA-based TF algorithm may not capture non-code contributions (documentation, issue triage, community management) that are critical to project survival [1]\\n- All commit-based algorithms systematically underestimate the importance of governance and community builders [18]\\n- Alias resolution: GitHub API email-to-user mapping misses developers with multiple accounts; median alias rate is 11% [1]\\n\\n**Review data gap** [12]:\\n- GH Archive lacks PullRequestReviewEvent, limiting bulk analysis of code review patterns [12]\\n- Reviews without comments are invisible in the archive [12]\\n\\n**Survival definition** [1]:\\n- Current definition (new TF developer arrives) may miss projects that survive through distributed maintenance without a single new core developer\\n- Does not capture \\\"zombie\\\" projects that have minimal activity but haven't formally died\\n\\n**Causal inference**:\\n- Observational studies cannot establish causality \u2014 projects that survive may have inherent characteristics that both enable survival and attract new developers\\n\\n#### 7.2 Generalizability\\n\\n- All major studies focus on GitHub projects; findings may not generalize to GitLab, Bitbucket, or self-hosted repositories\\n- Long-term survival beyond the observation window of existing studies is unknown\\n- Language-specific patterns may exist (studies covered 6 languages but did not analyze differences)\\n\\n### 8. CONFIDENCE ASSESSMENT\\n\\n**High confidence**:\\n- TFDD definition and 1-year threshold selection (validated through sensitivity analysis) [1]\\n- Basic survival statistics from Avelino et al. and Nourry et al. (large samples, clear methodology) [1, 3]\\n- GitHub API capabilities for commits and merges (well-documented) [8, 9, 14]\\n- AVL algorithm superiority (validated against human oracle) [18]\\n- Organizational ownership moderating effect (large sample of 5,762 projects) [20]\\n\\n**Medium confidence**:\\n- The relationship between project size and survival (contradictory findings between Avelino and Nourry) [1, 3]\\n- The predictive power of fade curve shape (not yet empirically tested as a specific variable)\\n- The adequacy of commit-based metrics for capturing full involvement (known to miss non-code contributions) [18]\\n- Write access proportion effect on survival (novel finding from single study) [20]\\n\\n**Low confidence**:\\n- The generalizability of findings beyond GitHub to other platforms\\n- The long-term survival of projects beyond the observation window of existing studies\\n- The extent to which value-related discussions predict turnover (single study) [7]\\n\\n### 9. SYNTHESIS: WHAT DETERMINES SURVIVAL?\\n\\nThe evidence converges on a multi-factorial model of project survival after founder departure:\\n\\n1. **Project maturity matters**: Older projects survive better (Nourry et al.) [3], likely because they have established communities, documentation, and governance structures.\\n\\n2. **Community depth matters**: Projects with more diverse contributor bases and lower write-access concentration are more resilient [20], but the relationship is complex \u2014 too much openness can reduce stability [20].\\n\\n3. **Organizational backing helps**: Organization-owned projects show different survival dynamics, with corporate resources providing a buffer against founder departure [20].\\n\\n4. **Succession quality matters**: Projects that attract new core developers who were already familiar with the codebase (52% of survivals) fare better than those relying on complete newcomers [1].\\n\\n5. **The shape of departure may matter**: Whether a founder leaves abruptly or gradually (with handoff) has not been systematically studied but is hypothesized to be a key predictor \u2014 this is the central question the scaffolding fade hypothesis aims to test.\\n\\n6. **Non-code contributions are critical**: Social interaction, code review, documentation, and testing are systematically underestimated by current metrics but are essential for project continuity [18].\\n\\n### FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS\\n\\n1. Can the **shape** of a founder's exit trajectory (abrupt departure vs. gradual fade vs. planned succession) predict survival better than static snapshots of project health at the time of departure?\\n\\n2. How do **non-code contributions** (issue triage, documentation, community management, code review) factor into project survival when the founder departs \u2014 and can these be reliably measured from GitHub data?\\n\\n3. What role does **organizational backing** (corporate sponsorship, foundation support, grant funding) play in mediating the relationship between founder departure and project survival, and how can this be operationalized as a control variable?\\n\\n4. Key findings: (1) TFDD occurs when ALL truck-factor developers abandon a project, with a 1-year inactivity threshold providing the best precision-improvement tradeoff [1]; (2) Among 1,932 popular projects, 16% faced TFDD and 41% survived; among 36,464 projects of all sizes, 89.6% faced TFDD but only 27% survived \u2014 revealing that smaller projects are far more fragile [1,3]; (3) Surviving projects tend to be older at TFDD time (1,267 vs 830 days), have more post-TFDD commits, and often attract a single new core developer (86% of survivals) [1,3]; (4) The AVL algorithm is the most accurate TF estimator, validated against a human oracle of 35 projects, but all commit-based algorithms miss non-code contributions (social interaction, code review, documentation, testing) [18]; (5) GitHub data extraction is feasible via REST/GraphQL APIs for commits, merges, and reviews, but GH Archive BigQuery lacks PullRequestReviewEvent data [8,12]; (6) Organizational ownership moderates the relationship between write access provisioning and survival \u2014 higher write access proportion increases novelty but reduces survival, and this effect is influenced by whether the project is organization-owned [20]; (7) Commit rights acquisition follows survival patterns: probability decreases with participation time, and developers who submit high-quality code, actively engage in code review, and make extensive contributions are more likely to gain commit rights [21]; (8) Recommended statistical models include Cox Proportional Hazards for time-to-survival analysis and logistic regression for binary survival outcomes, controlling for project age, star count, contributor diversity, file count, organizational ownership, and write access proportion.\",\n     5\t  \"answer\": \"## Methodology Grounding for Founder Fade Research: What Determines OSS Project Survival After Founder Departure?\\n\\n### 1. DEFINING THE CORE PHENOMENON: Truck Factor Developer Detachment (TFDD)\\n\\nThe foundational concept for studying founder departure in open-source projects is **Truck Factor Developer Detachment (TFDD)**, introduced and operationalized by Avelino, Constantinou, Valente, and Serebrenik (2019) [1]. The **Truck Factor (TF)** is defined as the minimal number of developers whose departure would put a project in serious trouble [1, 18]. TF is computed using the **Degree of Authorship (DOA)** metric: for each file, a developer's expertise is measured by whether they created the file and how many changes they made relative to others. The TF set comprises the minimal group of developers who are main authors (highest DOA) of at least 50% of the project's files [1, 18].\\n\\n**TFDD occurs when ALL TF developers abandon the project simultaneously** [1]. A developer is considered to have abandoned a project if their last commit occurred at least one year before the most recent repository commit [1]. This one-year threshold was selected from a sensitivity analysis comparing five thresholds (3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 1.5 years, 2 years), where the 1-year threshold achieved the highest harmonic mean of precision (82%) and improvement (55%) over the 6-month threshold [1].\\n\\nA project is classified as **surviving** if, after a TFDD event, it attracts at least one new TF developer who assumes maintenance \u2014 transitioning the project from an \\\"Inactive\\\" state back to \\\"Active\\\" [1].\\n\\n#### 1.1 TF Algorithm Landscape and Validation\\n\\nA comprehensive comparative study by Ferreira, Mombach, Valente, and Ferreira (2019) evaluated four TF algorithms against a human oracle constructed from surveys with developers of 35 open-source projects [18]:\\n\\n- **AVL Algorithm (Avelino et al., 2016)**: Uses DOA (Degree of Authorship) to identify file authors, then greedily removes top authors until 50% of files become abandoned. **Best accuracy**: median error of 1 developer, correctly identifying TF for 100% of TF=1 projects [18].\\n\\n- **RIG Algorithm (Rigby et al., 2016)**: Uses git-blame (line-level authorship) with random sampling (1,000 iterations). **Non-deterministic**: produces different results across runs, with dispersion ranging from 3 to 21 developers. Failed to produce results for large projects (symfony/symfony, saltstack/salt) due to insufficient random sampling [18].\\n\\n- **CST Algorithm (Cosentino et al., 2015)**: Uses primary/secondary developer classification with knowledge thresholds. Performance depends on metric choice: \\\"multiple changes equally considered\\\" (MCEC) outperforms \\\"last change takes it all\\\" (LCTA), with 24 vs. 18 correct TF estimates [18].\\n\\n- **ZWK Algorithm (Zazworka et al., 2010)**: Original combinatorial approach testing all possible developer combinations. **Does not scale** to projects with many contributors [18].\\n\\n**Critical limitation identified**: All existing TF algorithms are commit-based and miss non-code contributions. A survey of 17 contributors (7 responses) revealed that key developers often contribute through: **social interaction** (mailing lists, issues, Stack Overflow, conferences \u2014 4 responses), **code review** (accepting/reviewing PRs \u2014 2 responses), **documentation** (2 responses), **testing** (2 responses), and **supporting tools** (plugins, installers, demos \u2014 1 response) [18]. This means TF-based founder identification systematically underestimates the importance of developers whose primary value is governance, community building, or quality assurance.\\n\\n#### 1.2 Relationship Between Truck Factor and Core Developers\\n\\nFerreira et al. (2019) compared TF developers against two Core Developer heuristics (Commit-Based: 80% of commits; LOC-Based: 80% of churn) [18]:\\n\\n- **Truck Factor is a subset of Core Developers**: In 94% of systems evaluated by the Commit-Based Heuristic, the TF set is the same as or contained within the Core Developers set [18].\\n- **AVL algorithm outperforms both heuristics**: The LOC-Based Heuristic is more accurate than Commit-Based, but neither matches AVL's precision [18].\\n- **Implication**: TF developers are the \\\"core of the core developers\\\" \u2014 the smallest group whose departure would cause the most damage [18].\\n\\n### 2. EMPIRICAL LANDSCAPE: HOW COMMON IS ABANDONMENT AND SURVIVAL?\\n\\n#### 2.1 Avelino et al. (2019) \u2014 Popular Projects\\n\\nIn a dataset of 1,932 popular GitHub projects (top-500 most-starred across 6 languages: JavaScript, Python, Ruby, C/C++, Java, PHP), 315 projects (16%) experienced at least one TFDD [1]. Of these, 128 projects (41%) survived by attracting new core developers [1].\\n\\n**Key patterns**:\\n- 66% of TFDDs occurred in projects with TF=1 (single core developer) [1]\\n- 59% of TFDDs happened in the first two years of development [1]\\n- 86% of survivals involved attracting a single new TF developer [1]\\n- 52% of new TF developers were existing contributors; 41% were newcomers [1]\\n- Surviving projects had significantly more post-TFDD commits (median: 505 vs. 126) and higher percentage of post-TFDD commits (56% vs. 15%) than non-surviving projects (p = 5.02\u00d710\u207b\u00b2\u00b2 and p = 2.04\u00d710\u207b\u00b3\u00b2, Cliff's delta d = 0.64 and d = 0.79) [1]\\n- Counterintuitively, surviving projects had FEWER developers (32 vs. 47, p = 2.2\u00d710\u207b\u2074), FEWER commits (384 vs. 694, p = 2.6\u00d710\u207b\u2074), and FEWER files (54 vs. 108) at the time of TFDD [1]\\n\\n**Qualitative findings from surveying 33 new maintainers**:\\n- Most new maintainers were aware of abandonment risks when they started contributing [<response clipped><NOTE>Due to the max output limit, only part of this file has been shown to you. (2019) study on Truck Factor Developer Detachment (TFDD), its 2025 large-scale replication by Nourry et al., and practical GitHub data extraction protocols. Key findings: (1) TFDD occurs when ALL truck-factor developers abandon a project, with a 1-year inactivity threshold providing the best precision-improvement tradeoff; (2) Among 1,932 popular projects, 16% faced TFDD and 41% survived; among 36,464 projects of all sizes, 89.6% faced TFDD but only 27% survived \u2014 revealing that smaller projects are far more fragile; (3) Surviving projects tend to be younger at TFDD time, have more post-TFDD commits, and often attract a single new core developer (86% of survivals); (4) GitHub data extraction is feasible via REST/GraphQL APIs for commits, merges, and reviews, but GH Archive BigQuery lacks PullRequestReviewEvent data; (5) Founder identification should combine repository creation metadata with earliest sustained contribution patterns; (6) Recommended statistical models include Cox Proportional Hazards for time-to-survival analysis and logistic regression for binary survival outcomes, controlling for project age, star count, contributor diversity, and file count.\",\n  \"answer\": \"## Methodology Grounding for Founder Fade Research: What Determines OSS Project Survival After Founder Departure?\\n\\n### 1. DEFINING THE CORE PHENOMENON: Truck Factor Developer Detachment (TFDD)\\n\\nThe foundational concept for studying founder departure in open-source projects is **Truck Factor Developer Detachment (TFDD)**, introduced and operationalized by Avelino, Constantinou, Valente, and Serebrenik (2019) [1]. The **Truck Factor (TF)** is defined as the minimal number of developers whose departure would put a project in serious trouble [1, 2]. TF is computed using the **Degree of Authorship (DOA)** metric: for each file, a developer's expertise is measured by whether they created the file and how many changes they made relative to others. The TF set comprises the minimal group of developers who are main authors (highest DOA) of at least 50% of the project's files [1].\\n\\n**TFDD occurs when ALL TF developers abandon the project simultaneously** [1]. A developer is considered to have abandoned a project if their last commit occurred at least one year before the most recent repository commit [1]. This one-year threshold was selected from a sensitivity analysis comparing five thresholds (3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 1.5 years, 2 years), where the 1-year threshold achieved the highest harmonic mean of precision (82%) and improvement (55%) over the 6-month threshold [1].\\n\\nA project is classified as **surviving** if, after a TFDD event, it attracts at least one new TF developer who assumes maintenance \u2014 transitioning the project from an \\\"Inactive\\\" state back to \\\"Active\\\" [1].\\n\\n### 2. EMPIRICAL LANDSCAPE: HOW COMMON IS ABANDONMENT AND SURVIVAL?\\n\\n**Avelino et al. (2019) \u2014 Popular Projects** [1]: In a dataset of 1,932 popular GitHub projects (top-500 most-starred across 6 languages), 315 projects (16%) experienced at least one TFDD. Of these, 128 projects (41%) survived by attracting new core developers. Key patterns:\\n- 66% of TFDDs occurred in projects with TF=1 (single core developer) [1]\\n- 59% of TFDDs happened in the first two years of development [1]\\n- 86% of survivals involved attracting a single new TF developer [1]\\n- 52% of new TF developers were existing contributors; 41% were newcomers [1]\\n- Surviving projects had significantly more post-TFDD commits (median: 505 vs. 126) and higher percentage of post-TFDD commits (56% vs. 15%) than non-surviving projects [1]\\n- Counterintuitively, surviving projects had FEWER developers (32 vs. 47), FEWER commits (384 vs. 694), and FEWER files (54 vs. 108) at the time of TFDD [1]\\n\\n**Nourry et al. (2025) \u2014 Large-Scale Replication** [3]: Replicating Avelino's methodology on 36,464 projects (minimum 20 stars, 10 contributors, 2 years of history), they found dramatically different rates:\\n- 89.65% of projects faced at least one TFDD (vs. 16% in Avelino) \u2014 the difference attributed to including smaller, less popular projects [3]\\n- Only 27% of abandoned projects survived (vs. 41%) \u2014 smaller projects are less likely to attract new core developers [3]\\n- 70% of TFDDs occurred within the first three years [3]\\n- Most projects rely on a single core developer [3]\\n- The only metric showing a clear difference between surviving and non-surviving projects was **project age at TFDD**: surviving projects were older (1,267 days vs. 830 days) [3]\\n\\n**Contradiction and Resolution**: The disparity between Avelino's 16% and Nourry's 89.6% TFDD rate is explained by sample composition. Avelino studied only the top-500 most-starred projects per language \u2014 elite projects with large communities. Nourry included projects with as few as 20 stars, capturing the long tail of smaller projects where abandonment is the norm [3]. This suggests that **project popularity and community size are critical confounding variables**.\\n\\n### 3. WHAT PREDICTS SURVIVAL? EMPIRICAL FINDINGS\\n\\nThe empirical literature identifies several factors associated with project survival after founder departure:\\n\\n**Project characteristics** [1, 3]:\\n- **Age at TFDD**: Older projects survive better (Nourry et al.: 1,267 vs. 830 days) [3]\\n- **Post-TFDD activity**: Surviving projects show substantially more commits after TFDD [1]\\n- **Size paradox**: Avelino found surviving projects were smaller at TFDD time, while Nourry found minor differences in size \u2014 suggesting the relationship may be non-linear or context-dependent [1, 3]\\n\\n**Human and social factors** [1]:\\n- New maintainers were often already aware of abandonment risks when they started contributing [1]\\n- Their own usage of the system was the primary motivation to take over [1]\\n- Human and social factors played a key role in the transition [1]\\n- Lack of time and difficulty obtaining push access were the main barriers [1]\\n\\n**Developer turnover patterns** [4, 5]:\\n- Ferreira et al. found larger projects and organization-owned projects showed higher core developer turnover rates [4]\\n- Lin et al. found developers with higher codebase ownership are more likely to stay [5]\\n- Calefato et al. found 45% of core developers completely disengage for at least one year, with 35-55% returning [6]\\n\\n**Value-related discussions** [7]: Jamieson, Yamashita, and Foong (2024) showed that value-related discussions in GitHub issues can predict contributor turnover, suggesting that social dynamics and value alignment matter beyond pure code metrics [7].\\n\\n### 4. DATA EXTRACTION PIPELINE: TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY\\n\\n**Three-Channel Involvement Trajectories**:\\n\\n1. **Commits**: Feasible via both REST API (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits`) and GraphQL API (`repository.commits` connection). REST API returns 30 commits per page with pagination; GraphQL allows flexible filtering by author and date range. Rate limits: 5,000 requests/hour (REST, authenticated) or 5,000 points/hour (GraphQL) [8, 9].\\n\\n2. **Merges**: Identifiable via REST API (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls?state=closed`) \u2014 the `merged_by` field identifies who performed the merge. GraphQL offers `repository.pullRequests` with `mergedBy` field. The `PullRequestEvent` in GH Archive contains merge information [10, 11].\\n\\n3. **Reviews**: REST API (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pull_number}/reviews`) returns review data per PR. GraphQL offers `pullRequest.reviews` connection. **Critical limitation**: GH Archive BigQuery does NOT collect `PullRequestReviewEvent` \u2014 only `PullRequestReviewCommentEvent` is available [12]. Reviews without comments are invisible in the archive. For comprehensive review data, the REST or GraphQL API must be used directly.\\n\\n**Bulk Extraction Options**:\\n\\n- **GH Archive BigQuery**: Contains hourly GitHub event dumps since 2011. Event types include: PushEvent, PullRequestEvent, PullRequestReviewCommentEvent, IssueCommentEvent, CreateEvent, DeleteEvent, ForkEvent, ReleaseEvent, WatchEvent, and others [13]. Free tier allows 1 TB of queries per month. Best for commit and PR merge analysis, but NOT for comprehensive review data.\\n\\n- **GitHub REST API**: 5,000 requests/hour for authenticated users. Suitable for per-repository extraction but requires careful rate-limit management for large cohorts.\\n\\n- **GitHub GraphQL API**: 5,000 points/hour with complex scoring based on node counts. More efficient for complex queries but requires query optimization [8].\\n\\n**Recommendation**: Use GH Archive BigQuery for commit and merge history at scale, supplemented by targeted REST/GraphQL API calls for review data on the specific project cohort.\\n\\n### 5. FOUNDER AND DEPARTURE IDENTIFICATION PROTOCOLS\\n\\n**Founder Definition**:\\n- **Primary method**: Repository creator (GitHub API: `repository.owner` and `repository.createdAt`) [14]\\n- **Secondary method**: Earliest sustained contributor \u2014 the developer with the most commits in the first 6-12 months of project history [1]\\n- **Pitfalls**: Multiple early contributors in team projects; organizational repositories where the \\\"creator\\\" is a bot or organization account; forks where the original founder is not the fork creator\\n\\n**Departure Detection**:\\n- **Standard threshold**: 1 year of inactivity (last commit > 1 year before most recent repo commit) [1]\\n- **Alternative thresholds**: 3 months, 6 months (higher false positive rate), 1.5-2 years (higher false negative rate) [1]\\n- **Recommendation**: Use 1-year threshold as primary, with sensitivity analysis at 6-month and 1.5-year thresholds\\n\\n**Control Variables** (confounding factors to include in models) [1, 3, 4]:\\n- Project age at time of TFDD\\n- Total star count\\n- Number of contributors\\n- Number of files and commits\\n- Programming language\\n- Organizational vs. individual ownership\\n- Contributor diversity (number of distinct contributors)\\n- Historical activity patterns (commit frequency before TFDD)\\n\\n### 6. STATISTICAL ANALYSIS FRAMEWORK\\n\\n**Recommended Models**:\\n\\n1. **Cox Proportional Hazards**: For time-to-survival analysis \u2014 modeling the hazard of project death as a function of founder fade trajectory shape, controlling for covariates [15]\\n\\n2. **Logistic Regression**: For binary survival outcome (survived vs. did not survive) with features derived from involvement trajectories [1]\\n\\n3. **Mann-Whitney U Test**: For comparing distributions of metrics between surviving and non-surviving projects (as used in Avelino et al.) [1]\\n\\n4. **Survival curves (Kaplan-Meier)**: For visualizing survival probability over time post-TFDD\\n\\n**Feature Engineering from Trajectories**:\\n- Share of activity over time (monthly commits/merges/reviews as fraction of total)\\n- Fade curve shape (linear decline, step function, gradual taper)\\n- Time to last contribution\\n- Whether departure was abrupt (step) or gradual (fade)\\n- Presence of succession (new developer ramping up as founder ramps down)\\n\\n### 7. LIMITATIONS AND OPEN QUESTIONS\\n\\n- **TF algorithm limitations**: The DOA-based TF algorithm may not capture non-code contributions (documentation, issue triage, community management) that are critical to project survival [1]\\n- **Alias resolution**: The GitHub API email-to-user mapping misses developers with multiple accounts; median alias rate is 11% [1]\\n- **Review data gap**: GH Archive lacks PullRequestReviewEvent, limiting bulk analysis of code review patterns [12]\\n- **Survival definition**: Current definition (new TF developer arrives) may miss projects that survive through distributed maintenance without a single new core developer\\n- **Causal inference**: Observational studies cannot establish causality \u2014 projects that survive may have inherent characteristics that both enable survival and attract new developers\\n\\n### 8. CONFIDENCE ASSESSMENT\\n\\n**High confidence**: TFDD definition, 1-year threshold selection, basic survival statistics from Avelino et al. and Nourry et al., GitHub API capabilities for commits and merges.\\n\\n**Medium confidence**: The relationship between project size and survival (contradictory findings between studies), the predictive power of fade curve shape (not yet empirically tested), the adequacy of commit-based metrics for capturing full involvement.\\n\\n**Low confidence**: The generalizability of findings beyond GitHub to other platforms, the long-term survival of projects beyond the observation window of existing studies.\\n\\n### FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS\\n\\n1. Can the **shape** of a founder's exit trajectory (abrupt departure vs. gradual fade vs. planned succession) predict survival better than static snapshots of project health at the time of departure?\\n\\n2. How do **non-code contributions** (issue triage, documentation, community management, code review) factor into project survival when the founder departs \u2014 and can these be reliably measured from GitHub data?\\n\\n3. What role does **organizational backing** (corporate sponsorship, foundation support, grant funding) play in mediating the relationship between founder departure and project survival, and how can this be operationalized as a control variable?\\n\",\n  \"sources\": [\n    {\n      \"index\": 1,\n      \"url\": \"https://pure.tue.nl/ws/files/128584841/ESEM2019.pdf\",\n      \"title\": \"On the abandonment and survival of open source projects: An empirical investigation (Avelino, Constantinou, Valente, Serebrenik, 2019)\",\n      \"summary\": \"Foundational study defining TFDD, establishing 1-year abandonment threshold, analyzing 1,932 popular GitHub projects.
